181.event_title: Young Benjamin Franklin resolves to speak ill of no one
181.place: At sea, on the voyage from London to Philadelphia
181.event: In 1726, aged twenty and returning from London to Philadelphia after a period of youthful mistakes he later called errata, Benjamin Franklin drew up a written Plan of Conduct for his future life. Its fourth resolution was to speak ill of no one, even when the criticism would be true, and instead to excuse the faults he heard charged against others and to speak all the good he knew of everybody. The original manuscript is lost, but the text survives in an early printed copy reproduced in The Papers of Benjamin Franklin.
181.explanation: Franklin, who openly admitted his own early failings, singled out refraining from speaking ill of others as one of the few rules he set himself for life.
181.tie_back: The kural says that even a man with many faults has something good if it can be said that he does not speak ill of others behind their backs, and Franklin made that one restraint a cornerstone of his self-reform.
181._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it records a resolution against backbiting, not a community's verdict on an otherwise faulty man.

182.event: Procopius of Caesarea served as secretary to the general Belisarius and became the official historian of Emperor Justinian's reign, writing the Wars and a work called Buildings that praised Justinian's building projects. At the same time he secretly composed the Anecdota, or Secret History, a fierce attack on Justinian, Empress Theodora, Belisarius and his wife Antonina, saying it contained what he could not write openly for fear of the rulers. It was not published until after his death.
182.explanation: The same author praised his rulers in public and savaged them in private, and the Secret History is now a famous example of hidden disparagement behind a flattering front.
182.tie_back: The kural condemns tearing a person down behind his back while showing him a false smile to his face, and Procopius wrote praise for the court in public and invective against it in secret.
182._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's two-faced backbiter, though scholars still debate the work's exact purpose.

183.event_title: Irena Sendler refuses to give the Gestapo any names
183.event: Irena Sendler, a Warsaw social worker who headed the children's section of the underground Council to Aid Jews (Zegota), helped smuggle Jewish children out of the Warsaw Ghetto and place them in hiding. Arrested by the Gestapo in October 1943, she was interrogated under harsh mistreatment and pressed to give up the names of the organisation's leaders and the hidden children, but she never revealed the names of the children or her colleagues. She was sentenced to death, but Zegota bribed an official to release her, and she resumed her underground work.
183.explanation: Sendler could have bought her life by speaking against others, and she chose to face death instead.
183.tie_back: The kural says it is better to die than to live by speaking against others, and Sendler accepted a death sentence rather than save herself by betraying the people who depended on her.
183._accuracy_note: A strong picture of choosing death over speaking against others, but informing under duress is not quite the habitual backbiting the kural describes.

184.event: In 390 CE, after Emperor Theodosius I ordered a reprisal at Thessalonica that led to a massacre of its citizens, Bishop Ambrose of Milan wrote to the emperor directly, telling him he could not excuse the act and that he would not celebrate the Eucharist in his presence until the emperor repented. Ambrose required Theodosius to do public penance. After some hesitation the emperor complied and was readmitted to communion at Christmas 390.
184.explanation: Ambrose rebuked the most powerful man in the empire openly and in his own name, rather than undermining him in secret, and the emperor accepted the rebuke.
184.tie_back: The kural says harsh words spoken to a person's face are better than thoughtless words behind his back, and Ambrose chose to confront the emperor directly.
184._accuracy_note: A strong example of open, face-to-face rebuke, though the kural's main point is the contrast with backbiting, which is implied rather than shown here.

185.event_title: Richard Owen's anonymous review of the Origin of Species
185.event: Richard Owen, Britain's most eminent anatomist and a colleague of Charles Darwin for twenty years, wrote a very long anonymous review attacking On the Origin of Species, published in the Edinburgh Review in 1860. Britannica notes that Owen misquoted passages, altering words inside quotation marks, and that he was moved by a sense that his own preeminence was about to be lost. Darwin privately called the review extremely malignant and clever, and wrote to Charles Lyell of how painful it was to be hated so intensely by Owen.
185.explanation: A great scientist who stood for impartial learning revealed, through a hidden attack on a colleague, a pettiness that damaged his own lasting reputation.
185.tie_back: The kural says the meanness of backbiting shows that a man's heart is not truly given to virtue, however much he speaks of it, and Owen's anonymous attack exposed the gap between his public standing and his conduct.
185._accuracy_note: A strong case of a respected figure exposed by an anonymous attack, though Owen's moral talk is not the focus of the sources.

186.event_title: James Callender turns his pen on Thomas Jefferson
186.event: The journalist James Thomson Callender had attacked John Adams and the Federalists in pamphlets such as The Prospect Before Us (1800), with financial help from Thomas Jefferson, and was jailed under the Sedition Act. After Jefferson became president, Callender expected a reward, including the post of postmaster of Richmond, and when it did not come he felt betrayed. In 1802, writing in the Richmond Recorder, he turned the same invective on Jefferson, publishing damaging allegations about Jefferson's private life and the letters showing Jefferson had given him money.
186.explanation: Jefferson had helped sponsor a writer whose trade was attacking others' reputations, and that writer ended by selecting and publishing the most damaging charges against Jefferson himself.
186.tie_back: The kural warns that one who spreads others' faults will have his own worst faults hunted out and told, and Jefferson's support for Callender's attacks came back on him in exactly that way.
186._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of slander rebounding on its sponsor, though historians differ over how far Jefferson directed Callender's earlier attacks.

187.place: Wootton, Staffordshire, England, and Paris, France
187.event: In 1766 the philosopher David Hume brought Jean-Jacques Rousseau, then facing persecution on the Continent, to England and found him a refuge at Wootton in Staffordshire. Rousseau became convinced, wrongly, that Hume was at the centre of a plot to mock and dishonour him, and spread accounts of Hume's bad faith in letters that circulated in Paris. Hume answered by publishing their correspondence as A Concise and Genuine Account of the Dispute, and the friendship ended in a public quarrel.
187.explanation: Suspicion and accusatory talk turned a protector into an enemy and made the quarrel the talk of literary Europe.
187.tie_back: The kural says those who cannot build friendship through warm, cheerful words fall back on words that divide and drive away even their own friends, and Rousseau's accusations cost him his greatest benefactor.
187._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: divisive speech destroyed a friendship, but the sources trace Rousseau's suspicions to his troubled state of mind rather than to a lack of social skill.

188.event_title: Truman Capote publishes La Cote Basque 1965
188.event: In November 1975 Esquire magazine published La Cote Basque 1965, a chapter from Truman Capote's unfinished novel Answered Prayers. Capote's wealthy society friends, whom he called his swans, recognised themselves as thinly disguised characters whose private secrets, confided to him over years of friendship, were exposed. Most of them cut him off, and Babe Paley, his closest friend among them, never spoke to him again.
188.explanation: Capote treated the confidences of his closest friends as material to broadcast, and in doing so lost nearly all of them.
188.tie_back: The kural asks what a person who broadcasts the faults even of his intimates will not do to strangers, and Capote's friends, seeing their own secrets in print, drew exactly that conclusion.
188._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a man who published the faults of his closest friends and lost their trust.

189.event_title: Pietro Aretino, the scourge of princes
189.event: The writer Pietro Aretino settled in Venice in 1527 after making many enemies in Rome. His satirical attacks on the powerful often amounted to blackmail, and he called himself the scourge of princes. Kings and nobles who feared his satire or wanted his praise sent him gifts, and he grew wealthy and lived in style in Venice until his death in 1556.
189.explanation: Aretino prospered for decades by trading on what he might say about people, a puzzle that his contemporaries and later historians have noted.
189.tie_back: The kural wonders whether the earth bears the weight of the man who speaks base words of others only out of its own patience, and Aretino lived comfortably for decades on such words.
189._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Aretino's satire was largely open and signed rather than backbiting, though his comfortable life fits the kural's ironic wonder.

190.event_title: Willy Brandt kneels at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial
190.event: On 7 December 1970, the day West Germany signed the Treaty of Warsaw with Poland, Chancellor Willy Brandt laid a wreath at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising and then, unplanned, knelt in silence before it. Brandt, who had himself opposed the Nazis from exile, later said he had wanted to ask forgiveness in the name of the German people. The Nobel Committee cited the gesture when it awarded him the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize.
190.explanation: Instead of dwelling on others' wrongs, a German leader publicly acknowledged his own nation's guilt, and the gesture became a lasting symbol of reconciliation.
190.tie_back: The kural asks whether any harm could remain if people saw their own faults as clearly as others', and Brandt's gesture shows how facing one's own faults can open the way to healing.
190._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shows a nation's leader facing its own faults, while the kural concerns individual self-examination as the cure for backbiting.
